planting.note: Direct sow into saturated paddy beds or consistently flooded rows once soil has warmed; this landrace is adapted to a short, cool-altitude growing window rather than tropical lowland heat.

directions: Bhutanese red rice is a semi-milled japonica landrace traditionally grown in Himalayan valleys such as Paro, Punakha, Wangdue Phodrang, and the Tang valley of Bumthang, at elevations among the highest at which rice is cultivated anywhere in the world. The unpolished bran layer gives the grain a reddish-brown husk that cooks to a soft pink-red color, with a firm, slightly sticky bite and an earthy, nutty flavor distinct from lowland tropical rices. Its short, cool-adapted growing window makes it worth trialing in temperate gardens with a long, mild summer and a flooded or continuously saturated bed. Harvest when seed heads droop and grains have hardened, then dry thoroughly before milling lightly to preserve the bran layer that gives the rice its color and flavor.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Bhutan country profile
Lotus Foods product literature on Himalayan red rice

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; transplant once nights stay reliably above 55°F.

directions: Sha Ema is the everyday chili of Bhutanese cooking, a Capsicum annuum type in the general cayenne-to-Anaheim size range that is treated as a primary vegetable rather than a garnish, most famously stewed with melting yak or cow cheese to make ema datshi. Fruits are used fresh and green, allowed to ripen to red, or washed in hot water and sun-dried on rooftops into a wrinkled white-tan form that keeps through the Himalayan winter. Grow it as a standard garden pepper in full sun and well-drained soil, harvesting continuously through the season for fresh use while setting aside the latest red fruits for drying. Because Bhutanese cooks lean on volume and immediacy of heat more than extreme pungency, this variety performs best picked young and used generously rather than left to fully dry on the plant.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; transplant once nights stay reliably above 55°F.

directions: Nubi Ema takes its name from Nubi Gewog in Bhutan's Trongsa Dzongkhag, where this chili has long been grown as a sharper-flavored counterpart to the more common Sha Ema. Similar in fruit shape and plant habit to Sha Ema, it carries noticeably more heat and is prized for exactly that extra bite, most often dried and worked into ezay, the fiery Bhutanese chili-and-cheese condiment, as well as pickles and simmered stews. Grow it exactly as a standard garden Capsicum annuum pepper, in full sun with even moisture, and plan to harvest both green and fully red fruit since Bhutanese kitchens use both stages. Sun-dry the ripe red fruit on racks or rooftops for a shelf-stable winter supply that concentrates the variety's characteristic fire.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in frost-free, well-drained soil; grafted trees reach bearing age in about 4-5 years versus far longer for seedlings.

directions: Keo Romeat is Cambodia's dominant commercial mango, accounting for roughly 80 percent of the country's production, grown widely in Kampong Speu, Battambang, and Oddar Meanchey provinces. Fruit ripens from deep green to golden-yellow with vivid orange, low-to-medium-fiber flesh carrying a balanced sweet flavor and rich aroma, and well-managed trees can produce up to three flushes of fruit per year. Plant a grafted tree in full sun on deep, well-drained soil, protecting young trees from frost and wind until established, since mango will not tolerate freezing temperatures at any age. Beyond fresh eating, Keo Romeat's flesh holds up well to processing, and much of the Cambodian crop is dried or frozen as IQF cubes for export.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Cambodia mango value chain materials

common_name: Sen Kra Ob Cambodian Fragrant Rice

planting.note: Direct sow into flooded or continuously saturated paddy beds; unlike Cambodia's classic photoperiod-sensitive jasmine rices, this variety is non-seasonal and can be sown across multiple windows in a long warm season.

directions: Sen Kra Ob (officially designated SKO 01) was developed and released by the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute as a short-duration, non-photoperiod-sensitive fragrant rice, in contrast to the long-season, daylight-triggered jasmine landraces Cambodia is best known for. It produces long, slender, naturally aromatic kernels with a soft cooked texture reminiscent of jasmine rice, and because it isn't tied to a single seasonal planting window it supports multiple harvests a year, commonly timed around April and July in Cambodia. Grow it as a conventional flooded or saturated-bed paddy rice, keeping the bed consistently wet through tillering and grain fill, then draining before harvest once grain heads droop and harden. Its shorter life cycle compared to traditional jasmine types makes it a practical choice where the warm season is long but not quite long enough for slower landraces.
sources: Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI) variety releases
International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) regional variety reporting

planting.note: Sow fresh seed directly where it will grow; this palm resents transplanting once its deep taproot establishes, and trees need roughly 12-20 years before they are tapped for sap.

directions: This is the sugar-palm landrace grown in Cambodia's Kampong Speu province, locally called derm thnot, whose sap is tapped from the flower stalks and boiled down into Skor Thnot, a palm sugar protected as a Cambodian geographical indication since 2010 and by the EU since 2019. Sap is collected mainly in the dry season from December to May by climbing the tall, slow-growing trunk daily to collect and re-cut the flower stalks, then reducing the sap over wood fires into soft blocks or granules with a low glycemic index and notes of caramel, honey, and light smoke. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives in open, full-sun conditions on well-drained soil, tolerating the long Cambodian dry season far better than most fruiting palms. Because it takes well over a decade to reach tapping age and grows to full canopy palm size, it is a multigenerational planting rather than a quick garden crop.
sources: Cambodian Ministry of Commerce geographical indication registry
European Union protected geographical indication registration for Kampong Speu Palm Sugar
